bib.title: Chapter 3. The Spectrum of LLM Adaptation for Agents: RAG to Fine-tuning (Agentic Architectural Patterns)
bib.venue: Packt (book chapter); authors and year are not printed in the chapter PDF

read.by: main-session (source-reader dispatch refused: concurrent subagent limit)

question: How should a general LLM be specialised for an agent role, and how are specialised agents organised and governed?
contributions: Hierarchical architecture: orchestrator, sub-agent, tool, AgentTool
Three RAG scenarios (support, financial analyst, compliance) with RAG spectrum mapped to maturity
FFT versus PEFT comparison, SFT versus unsupervised fine-tuning
In-context learning with a feedback-analyzer example

results.claim: An AgentTool is a whole fine-grained agent (own state, workflow and tools) packaged and exposed as a tool to other agents; a plain tool is a stateless wrapper around one function.
results.setup: Design definition with a customer-onboarding orchestrator example (KYC agent, credit-check agent, send_email tool); no measurement.
results.quote: an AgentTool is a complete, self-contained, fine-grained

results.claim: A tool is the most basic building block of action: stateless, one specific atomic action.
results.quote: A tool is the most basic building block of action.

results.claim: Callbacks on model, tool and agent start and end create an audit trail of prompts, arguments, results, errors and run duration.
results.quote: create an immutable audit trail, recording which agent called which

results.claim: A support agent without RAG gives generic advice for a post-update error; with RAG over a service bulletin it names the fix (patch v1.2.3).
results.setup: Hypothetical ProWidget X scenario, no evaluation.
results.quote: Error E404 on ProWidget X units post-June 25th firmware push (v1.2.2).

results.claim: A compliance agent with RAG finds a $50,000 external threshold and a $25,000 internal threshold that a $75,000 wire breaches, and holds the transaction.
results.setup: Hypothetical figures for Countries A and B; illustrative only.
results.quote: All outbound wire transfers from Country A exceeding $50,000 USD to

results.claim: PEFT reduces the risk of catastrophic forgetting and lets many agent specialisations share one base model; FFT may reach a higher ceiling at very high cost.
results.quote: significantly reduce the risk of catastrophic forgetting

results.claim: In-context learning adapts behaviour with examples in the prompt and no weight change; larger context windows allow more examples.
results.setup: Product-feedback analyzer example with three few-shot examples and JSON output; qualitative.
results.quote: Crucially, this occurs without requiring any changes to the model

results.claim: A diagnostic agent flags a diagnosis for mandatory senior review when model confidence is low (example threshold below 70 percent).
results.setup: Illustrative threshold; the chapter does not discuss calibration of stated confidence.
results.quote: will flag the diagnosis for mandatory review by a senior technician

limits: No measured results; every scenario is hypothetical with invented figures.
Calibration of LLM confidence scores is assumed, not examined.
The six-level agentic maturity model is the authors' framework, not validated.
RAG, FFT/PEFT and ICL are described at overview depth with no benchmarks.
practices: Package a sub-agent as an AgentTool; keep plain tools for atomic deterministic steps.
Log model, tool and agent start and end events as callbacks.
Ground outputs: cite sources, cross-check critical claims, use confidence to escalate, ask when the input is ambiguous.
Use PEFT first when many specialised agents share a base model; reserve FFT for the deepest specialisation.

terms.definition: A complete fine-grained agent exposed as a tool for other agents.
Systematically connecting model output to verifiable information sources.

lineage.work: LoRA, adapter tuning, prefix- and prompt-tuning
